rounds.proof_sketch: Original: (out_features < 1024) ? out_features : 1024. Mutated: (out_features < 1025) ? out_features : 1024. The only differing case is out_features=1024: Original takes else-branch returning 1024; Mutated takes if-branch returning out_features=1024. Both yield identical threads_count=1024 for ALL values of out_features.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation from `< 1024` to `< 1025` creates a semantically equivalent expression. For out_features < 1024, both conditions are TRUE, yielding out_features. For out_features = 1024, original condition is FALSE (returns 1024) while mutated condition is TRUE (returns out_features which IS 1024). For out_features > 1024, both conditions are FALSE, yielding 1024. Thus for every possible value of out_features, the threads_count computed is identical. No input value manipulation can expose a difference because the expressions are mathematically equivalent.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable because the original and mutated expressions are semantically equivalent across all possible values of out_features. The boundary case that differs (out_features=1024) produces identical output values via different code paths (else-branch returning literal 1024 vs if-branch returning out_features which equals 1024).
rounds.recommendations: This mutation exposes a weakness in constant perturbation operators - they should check if the perturbed constant results in semantically equivalent expressions. In this case, changing the boundary from 1024 to 1025 in a min(out_features, 1024) pattern is equivalent because when out_features equals the boundary value, both branches return the same value.
